title: A better client reply
description: Turn a messy site-visit note into a proposal and a three-line WhatsApp reply.
problem: A client conversation is scattered across messages. Writing a proposal takes the evening.
opportunity: Start with a useful first draft and spend your time refining the offer.
firstStep: Use the fictional client notes. Change one preference and check the reply.
prompt:
You are an account manager at a Nairobi interior design studio.
Use the fictional site-visit notes below to draft a proposal email of no more
than 220 words to Mrs Wanjiru. Use five short sections: Your priorities,
Suggested approach, Timing, Budget, Next step.
Keep the tone warm and professional. The KES 450,000 figure is a client budget,
not our quote: do not invent prices or a price range. State that a costed
proposal follows measurements and supplier checks. Treat 15 December 2026 as
the client's requested completion date, subject to confirming scope and supply.
Keep the sister's potential kitchen project separate from this client's scope.
After the email, add a separate "Internal checks — remove before sending"
section listing missing facts and assumptions. Do not place internal checks
inside the customer-facing email.

Notes:
Mrs Wanjiru, 3BR in Kilimani, wants living room + dining redone. budget around
450k. likes warm colours, hates grey. has 2 dogs so no delicate fabrics. wants
it done before december 15 bcz family coming. current sofa she keeps. site visit
tuesday went ok, walls need repainting + one wall maybe wallpaper. mentioned
her sister also wants her kitchen done later.
followup:
Turn the customer-facing email into a three-line WhatsApp message. Keep the
budget and timing caveats. Mention durable, pet-friendly fabrics. No invented
prices, discounts or availability commitments.
checks: KES 450,000 stays a budget, not a made-up quote.
15 December stays a requested date, subject to confirmation.
The sister’s kitchen stays separate from the client’s project.

title: An answer you can trace
description: Turn a short cleaning RFQ into a checklist, then open the source behind an answer.
problem: The documents that matter are often the ones nobody has time to read.
opportunity: Find requirements quickly and inspect the passages that support them.
firstStep: Upload the fictional RFQ, select it as the only source and ask for a checklist.
prompt:
Using only the selected fictional RFQ, make a bidder checklist. Columns:
requirement; mandatory or optional; deadline if stated; supporting citation
and section identifier. Separate explicit rejection grounds from general
requirements. Do not infer extra mandatory conditions. If a detail is absent,
write "Not specified in the source". Finish with the three most important
clarifications we should obtain before quoting.
followup:
How many windows are there, what size are they, and can our team clean all of
them safely from ground level? Cite any supporting passage. If the RFQ does
not establish an answer, say so and draft one short clarification question.
checks: Submission closes 6 November at 12:00 noon EAT.
Window count, size and height are not specified.

title: What is your stock saying?
description: Find the biggest profit contributors, slow movers and a simple stock top-up.
problem: Sales sit in a spreadsheet while purchasing decisions happen on instinct.
opportunity: Calculate consistently and turn the table into questions worth investigating.
firstStep: Paste the supplied fictional data, then compare the answer with the checked totals.
prompt:
Act as a retail operations analyst explaining a fictional shop's data to its
owner. Use a calculation/data-analysis tool if available and tell me if it is
not available. Treat the following as a simplified classroom example.

Assume no restocking, returns, shrinkage, price changes or stockouts during the
30 days. Assume the next 30 days have the same demand, instant delivery and no
safety stock. Costs and sales prices use the same simplified tax basis.

Calculate per product:
1. Revenue = units sold × selling price.
2. Gross profit = units sold × (selling price - unit cost).
3. Closing stock = opening stock - units sold.
4. Sell-through percentage = units sold / opening stock × 100.
5. Top-up quantity = max(0, units sold - closing stock).

Give one table and the total revenue, cost of goods sold and gross profit.
Rank the top three products by total gross-profit contribution.
Define slow-moving as lowest sell-through percentage and name the bottom
three, noting ties. Explain the next actions in no more than five bullets.
Show the formulas and the worked calculation for rice and cooking oil.
State that overheads are absent, so net profit cannot be determined. State
which real-world information is missing before a purchasing decision.

Product,Opening stock,Units sold (30 days),Unit cost KES,Selling price KES
Basmati rice 2kg,120,95,310,380
Cooking oil 3L,80,70,720,850
Sugar 2kg,150,40,260,300
Laundry soap bar,200,35,45,60
Wheat flour 2kg,100,88,170,210
Tea leaves 500g,60,12,350,480
Toilet paper 10 pack,90,82,380,450
Instant noodles carton,40,8,900,1100
followup:
Create a horizontal bar chart of total gross-profit contribution by product,
sorted from largest to smallest. Label values in KES and use the title
"Gross profit from units sold — fictional 30-day example". Explain in two
sentences why a high margin percentage need not mean the most total profit.
checks: Cooking oil contributes the most gross profit: KES 9,100.
Overheads are absent. Net profit cannot be determined.

title: A small tool, built for you
description: Delegate a cleaning calculator, inspect its checks and try the finished result.
problem: You need a repeatable way to estimate a cleaning job without rebuilding the maths.
opportunity: Give Codex a goal, business rules and acceptance checks, then review its work.
firstStep: Start the build at the end of Demo 2. Return to the result after the stock demo.
prompt:
Build and test a working, phone-friendly cleaning quote calculator in this
demo folder. Deliver a self-contained quote-calculator.html file with its CSS
and JavaScript included. It must work offline with no external libraries,
images, fonts, services or network requests. Create the actual file, perform
the checks below using the tools available to you, and open or link the working
result for review. If an interactive HTML preview is available, show it too.

Business rules for this fictional training example:
- Floor area in square metres must be a finite number greater than zero.
- Visits per week: choose 1, 3 or 5.
- Windows: yes or no.
- Use exactly 52 / 12 weeks per month to estimate average monthly visits.
- Cleaning price: KES 18 per square metre per visit.
- Windows: a fixed KES 6,000 per month when selected.
- Subtotal = area × 18 × visits per week × 52 / 12 + windows fee.
- Apply an illustrative 16% VAT to the entire subtotal, including windows.
- Total = subtotal + illustrative VAT.
- Retain full precision during calculation; display currency to two decimals.

Show area, average visits per month, cleaning amount, windows amount, subtotal,
illustrative VAT and grand total, all clearly labelled. Explain that 52/12 is
an average estimate; actual calendar visits may differ. Label the rates and
tax assumption as fictional training inputs, not verified market or tax advice.
Default to 400 square metres, 3 visits per week and windows included. This
matches our fictional RFQ; do not claim it is a final commercial quote.
For invalid or missing area input, show a helpful error and no valid quote.
Use large text, clear form labels and a professional design.

Verify these cases before delivering the file:
100 m2, 3 visits/week, windows yes: subtotal KES 29,400; VAT KES 4,704;
grand total KES 34,104.
100 m2, 3 visits/week, windows no: grand total KES 27,144.
400 m2, 3 visits/week, windows yes: grand total KES 115,536.
Blank, zero, negative and non-numeric area: validation error, no valid quote.
Test the actual implemented calculation logic, not just a separate copy of
the formula. If browser tools are available, also check the form controls,
invalid inputs and a narrow phone viewport. Report which checks you actually
performed and any you could not perform. Give a brief delivery summary and
the path to the finished file. Do not publish or deploy it.
followup:
Add a "Print estimate" button. The print view must retain the inputs, amount
breakdown and training/assumption notes. Preserve every calculation rule and
rerun the same checks.
checks: Missing or invalid floor area produces an error, not a valid quote.
